name: Scutellaria baicalensis root extract
lead: Scutellaria baicalensis root extract comes from Baikal skullcap, a mint-family plant whose dried root (huangqin) is one of the 50 fundamental herbs of traditional Chinese medicine.[1] Its main flavonoids include baicalin, baicalein and wogonin.[1] In cosmetics it is used as an anti-inflammatory or brightening botanical.

Laboratory studies report antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, and a 2025 safety assessment reviewed its use as a cosmetic ingredient.[2][3][4] A case report documents allergic contact dermatitis to a cosmetic containing it.[5] Two small registered trials have tested creams for hyperpigmentation, though results were not located.

paras: In vitro studies report that a wogonin-rich fraction suppressed IL-1beta-induced inflammatory signalling in human osteoarthritic chondrocytes, and that root extracts protected lipid membranes from peroxidation in rat lung mitochondria.[2][3] These are non-skin models.

The International Journal of Toxicology published a safety assessment of S. baicalensis-derived ingredients as used in cosmetics in 2025.[4] A case report described allergic contact dermatitis to a cosmetic containing resveratrol and S. baicalensis root extract.[5] Wikipedia notes case reports of liver injury linked to oral supplements containing the plant.[1]

Two registered trials examined creams containing the extract for hyperpigmentation: a 2025 study of a huangqin cream (n=38) and a 2023 study of a topical cream for post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation in Malaysians (n=25).[6][7] Published outcomes were not found among the sources reviewed.

card.summary: Chinese skullcap root extract used as an anti-inflammatory or brightening ingredient, with small trials registered but little published human evidence.
card.note: Contact allergy reported; oral products linked to liver injury case reports.

quick.overview:
A root extract from Baikal skullcap, a staple of traditional Chinese medicine, now used in some skincare for anti-inflammatory or brightening claims.

Evidence is mostly lab studies; two small hyperpigmentation cream trials are registered.
quick.mechanism: Flavonoids such as baicalin and wogonin showed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity in cell and animal studies.
quick.risks: A case report describes contact allergy to a cosmetic containing it, and oral supplements have been linked to liver injury in case reports.
